answer: Each week the surveyor drills the sea ice at the marked stations and writes the thickness in the survey book, and no sled may cross until the gauge is read. A walnut thickness guessed from the shore fails the book: at the saffron of the drill the ice must measure what the surveyor recorded, and a guessed thickness drops a team through the floe. Forging the survey means drilling for a whole winter, measuring 170 stations and paying 12,100, while the tundra figure in the survey book is checked by every trail master, so ice whose thickness was never drilled is closed to all.
